title: Alternative Blindness
hook: The two options on the table can feel like the whole world when the useful third path is offstage.
counterintuition: A clear pair can make a decision feel disciplined while hiding the better move; before choosing A or B, inspect the choice set and force the missing option into view.
tryThisNow: For one live A-or-B decision, write a third possible action that neither side offers, then ask what would change if that option had been named first.
keyTakeaway: Do not mistake the presented pair for the full choice set. Look for the missing option before you choose.

breakdown.fastRead: A dispatch team debates two scripts for flood calls: send crews now or tell callers to wait. The site photo shows a blocked side road neither script mentions. Alternative blindness begins when the offered pair feels complete. A pair is not a choice set. The fix is to ask what option is missing before you pick between the visible two. Sometimes the right move is not A or B. It is a third path the frame kept out of sight.
breakdown.deepRead:
A menu gives you two plans, and both feel wrong. One is too costly. One is too thin. Because they are printed side by side, your mind starts acting as if the real task is to choose between them. You begin comparing flaws instead of asking why these are the only two plans in front of you.

Alternative blindness is a framing error. The presented pair captures attention so strongly that the missing option never gets a hearing. This can happen in a boardroom, a family argument, a lease deal, a medical choice, or a budget fight. The pair may be real, but it is not automatically complete. It may be the seller's pair, the loud person's pair, the rushed person's pair, or the pair that makes the institution's life easier.

The missing option can be the decision.

The correction is simple and awkward: pause before the comparison hardens. Ask what action is absent. Ask whether one option can be split, delayed, scaled, tested, delegated, or replaced. Ask who benefits if the choice stays as a pair. The goal is not endless creativity. It is to prevent the frame from deciding before judgment begins.

This matters because smart people can debate bad pairs with great skill. They can weigh pros and cons, score criteria, argue tradeoffs, and still miss the move that would have changed the problem. The warning sign is a sentence like, 'We have to choose one.' Maybe you do. But first, prove that the choice set is real.
breakdown.fullRead:
The travel insurer's pricing team sees two packages on the screen: cheap basic cover or expensive full cover. The blood-test panel for older travelers sits in the appendix, because nobody wants medical screening to slow the quote flow. The debate becomes clean. Basic loses money on a few claims. Full cover scares off healthy customers. The missing option is a screened middle tier, and it is invisible because the meeting was built around a pair.

Alternative blindness often enters through neatness. Two options are easy to compare. They create a tidy argument, a tidy vote, and a tidy slide. People feel decisive because the contrast is sharp. Yet the sharpness can be a trick of presentation. The frame may hide a scale, a sequence, a pilot, a hybrid, a delay, or a smaller reversible test.

Before you choose between two doors, check who built the hallway.

A podcast ad renewal can make the same mistake. The host either renews the full sponsor package or drops it. The airport board near the studio shows delayed flights, and the producer jokes that listeners are probably stuck somewhere with time to hear ads. The pair sounds complete until someone asks whether the renewal can move to two cities, two episodes, and a conversion test. The third path is not glamorous. It is better because it tests the claim without paying for the whole bet.

The awkward question is: what option would we invent if neither presented option were allowed? That question breaks the spell. If the answer is useless, fine. Return to the pair and choose. But often the answer reveals a path that was missing only because the room was moving too fast. A lab can retest one sample instead of accepting or rejecting the whole result. A charity can change donor timing instead of choosing between two campaign themes. A city can open cooling centers by heat-risk zone instead of choosing all sites or none.

There is a limit. Some decisions really are binary. A plane takes off or it does not. A contract is signed by a deadline or it expires. A medicine is given or withheld. Even then, alternative blindness can still matter upstream: different deadline, different dose, different backup, different information source, different person making the call. The final act may be binary, but the design around it often is not.

The practical move is to add one sentence to every serious A-or-B decision: 'The missing option might be...' Then force a visible mark. Put the third path on the page, even if it is ugly. Price it. Reject it if it fails. What matters is that the pair no longer gets to pretend it is the universe. Once the missing option has been named, choosing A or B becomes a decision instead of obedience to the frame.

examples.title: The flood script with a blocked side road
examples.scenario: A site photo of a flooded underpass is taped to the emergency dispatch script at 2:18 a.m. in the Ottawa operations room. Christine, the night supervisor on the river-flood desk, must decide between sending rescue crews now or telling callers to shelter. She circles alternative blindness on the photo, adds a third script for callers near the blocked side road, and has the dispatcher test that route before the next call.
examples.whatToDo: Look for the action the offered pair leaves unnamed, then put it into the live script.
examples.whyItMatters: A safety choice can look binary while the useful missing option is location-specific.

examples.title: The travel policy without a middle tier
examples.scenario: "Basic or full cover by noon," the pricing director says as a blood-test panel sits beside the Munich travel insurance file. Dennis must decide between raising every premium or cutting older travelers from the policy. He marks missing option beside the panel, proposes a screened middle tier, and changes the pricing memo while the actuary watches.
examples.whatToDo: Ask whether a screened or conditional option exists between two blunt products.
examples.whyItMatters: The pair can hide the policy design that would fit risk without overcharging everyone.

examples.title: The sponsor renewal with a smaller test
examples.scenario: The airport board flickers behind the podcast studio glass while delayed departures stack in yellow rows. Marion must decide between renewing the full ad package or dropping the sponsor before Monday's recording. She underlines presented pair on the sales sheet, offers a two-city test buy, and asks the host to judge renewals by conversions instead of the forced pair.
examples.whatToDo: Turn an all-or-nothing renewal into a bounded test when the full pair is too crude.
examples.whyItMatters: Presented pairs often make a partial experiment disappear.

examples.title: The lab result that needs a retest
examples.scenario: You are looking at a loan worksheet under a centrifuge schedule in a university lab meeting. Jonathan, the grant manager, must decide between buying a new analyzer or accepting the disputed result from the old one. He writes third path on the worksheet, funds a one-week outside retest, and changes the purchase vote in front of the principal investigator.
examples.whatToDo: Create a temporary third path when the visible pair jumps from acceptance to replacement.
examples.whyItMatters: A retest can resolve the choice without turning one odd result into a capital purchase.

examples.title: The donor campaign that ignores timing
examples.scenario: It took Adaeze two campaign previews in the Birmingham charity kitchen to see why the tasting spoon mattered. Donors loved the meal-photo concept, trustees preferred the statistics mailer, and both sides treated the choice set as fixed. She must decide which campaign goes live. She writes choice set beside the spoon, proposes sending the meal story after small gifts and the statistics after renewals, and changes the campaign calendar.
examples.whatToDo: Look for timing or sequencing when two messages both have a role.
examples.whyItMatters: The missing option may be not a third message, but a better order for the existing two.

examples.title: The heat map with the wrong binary
examples.scenario: Which matters more during a heat wave: opening every cooling center or only the cheapest five? Frank reviews a scoreboard still from last summer's emergency desk in a Phoenix city postmortem. He writes alternative on the still, marks neighborhoods where ambulance calls spiked, and changes the next map to open centers by heat-risk zone instead of the old all-or-five pair.
examples.whatToDo: Replace a crude binary with a risk-based choice set when public safety varies by place.
examples.whyItMatters: The absent alternative can be a map rule, not a compromise between two totals.

reviewCards.front: A decision is framed as A or B. What third option should be searched for?
reviewCards.back: Pause the forced pair and name at least one real alternative. The presented options may be a frame, not the full choice.

reviewCards.front: A pair feels clear and disciplined. What is the risk?
reviewCards.back: Clarity can hide alternative blindness. A clean pair may exclude the option that would fit the evidence.

reviewCards.front: What kinds of missing options should you look for?
reviewCards.back: Look for pilots, splits, delays, smaller tests, sequencing, delegation, location rules, and hybrid paths.

reviewCards.front: When is A or B acceptable?
reviewCards.back: After you can explain why the choice set is real and why plausible third paths fail the cost or evidence test.

reviewCards.front: What phrase should interrupt a forced pair?
reviewCards.back: Say, 'The missing option might be...' and put at least one third path on the page before choosing.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Inspect the choice set before choosing between the visible pair. Add, price, and reject or use a missing option deliberately.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a choice is presented as A or B, then I will ask what third path is absent before voting.
If two options both feel wrong, then I will write one split, delay, or small test before deciding.
If a proposal is framed as fund or cut, then I will ask whether scale, timing, or location creates another option.
If two people argue for opposite solutions, then I will name the shared problem and search for an option neither side proposed.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one A-or-B decision in your day. Add a third path to the page, price it quickly, and only then choose among the set.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review one past decision and ask which option was never named because the pair arrived too cleanly.

memorableLines.text: A pair is not a choice set.
The missing option can be the decision.
Before you choose between two doors, check who built the hallway.
